On GenAI, the court finds that grounded chatbots perform an information-retrieval function similar to general search engines, enough to bring GenAI inside the decree. | [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. Status functions imposed by collective acceptance carry deontic powers, and deontic powers are desire-independent reasons for action. Read it for the structure, not for an argument about collective intentionality: that is taken as a primitive and referred to his 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)), not defended here. |
| [LIT-489](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-489.md) | Institutions | North (1991), DOI-10.1257/jep.5.1.97. Institutions are "the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction": informal constraints (taboos, customs, codes of conduct) and formal rules (constitutions, laws, property rights). With technology they set transaction and production costs, and so the incentive structure of an economy. Tribal exchange, the Suq and the caravan trade did not evolve from within; early modern European trade did, through merchant law, bills of exchange, insurance and a state bound not to confiscate. Institutional change is path dependent because the institutional matrix has increasing returns. A narrative essay; the definition is stipulated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-392](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-392.md)); worth reading as the economist's canonical one-paragraph definition of institutions ("the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction") and as a compact statement of the transaction-cost and path-dependence programme. It is an essay, not an argument: the game-theoretic motivation is one paragraph, the history is narrative, and the definition is stipulated, not defended. For what an institution is, read it beside Hindriks & Guala ([LIT-481](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-481.md)), who take it as the exemplar of the rules account and say what it leaves out. |
| [LIT-494](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-494.md) | The Theory of Dyadic Morality: Reinventing Moral Judgment by Redefining Harm | Schein & Gray (2018), DOI-10.1177/1088868317698288. By its abstract: harm is an intuitively perceived continuum, not an objective matter, and acts are condemned in proportion to norm violation, negative affect and perceived harm, where harm is dyadic (an intentional agent damaging a vulnerable patient). Harm leads to condemnation and condemnation to perceived harm (the "dyadic loop"). The theory argues against intuitively harmless wrongs and modular foundations. Unread: the argument and evidence are not known here. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the PubMed abstract and Crossref record, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The SAGE PDF, listed as free to read, sits behind a bot challenge (HTTP 403); the PubMed record has no PMC copy; a University of North Carolina repository file returned by a search for the paper (cdr.lib.unc.edu/downloads/w9505f334) reset every connection, so what it holds is unknown; Semantic Scholar points only to the SAGE PDF, and CORE, OpenAlex and the Wayback Machine had no copy. It is the main harm-based rival to morality-as-cooperation, and what it argues is known here only from its abstract and from how other readings in this batch describe it. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-499](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-499.md) | Moral Foundations Theory: The Pragmatic Validity of Moral Pluralism | Graham et al. (2013), DOI-10.1016/B978-0-12-407236-7.00002-4. Moral Foundations Theory in full: a nativist, cultural-developmental, intuitionist and pluralist account with five foundations (Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity), each tied to an adaptive challenge and an existing evolutionary model. A decade of MFQ work finds liberals rely on Care and Fairness, conservatives on all five, across 12 world regions. Five criteria for "foundationhood" are proposed, and Liberty, Efficiency, Ownership and Honesty are named candidates. Harm monism (Gray) and fairness monism (Baumard) are rejected as Procrustean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md)); worth reading as the full statement of Moral Foundations Theory and as the text to check morality-as-cooperation's comparison against. It states the theory's four claims (nativism, cultural learning, intuitionism, pluralism), reviews a decade of MFQ findings, mostly on political ideology, and offers five criteria for what counts as a foundation. By its own table the Care foundation rests on kin selection and Fairness on Trivers' reciprocal altruism, and Ownership/theft is already a named candidate, so the claim that MFT omits kin altruism, reciprocal altruism and property does not survive this text. Sanctity, the foundation morality-as-cooperation excludes, is by the same table the one with the least evidence of innate preparedness. |
| [LIT-500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-500.md) | Morality beyond the WEIRD: How the nomological network of morality varies across cultures | Atari et al. (2023), DOI-10.1037/pspp0000470. The Moral Foundations Questionnaire-2: 36 items, six per foundation, for Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority and Purity, built and tested on 25 populations (N ≈ 8,700) in local languages. Equality and Proportionality correlate weakly (mean r = .21). Purity is the foundation most related to cultural distance from the U.S. (r = .43) and to religiosity. The individualizing–binding split appears in only three of 19 national networks. The MFQ-2 explains more variance in 30 criterion scores than the MFQ-1 (mean adjusted R² .37 against .30). | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-398](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-398.md)), from the APA accepted manuscript; worth reading as the current Moral Foundations measure (the MFQ-2) and the theory's current list of six foundations, with Fairness split into Equality and Proportionality, and as the place MFT answers morality-as-cooperation directly: Curry et al. 2019 "left out Purity as an important and less-WEIRD moral foundation". Its strongest evidence for that, Purity's association with cultural distance from the U.S., rests on the one subscale that fails its own measurement-invariance threshold. Its samples are online panels in 25 populations, not small-scale societies. |

| [LIT-719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-719.md) | Beyond Markets and States: Polycentric Governance of Complex Economic Systems | Ostrom (2009), Nobel lecture; AER 2010. Polycentric arrangements of many formally independent decision centres can perform better than a single hierarchy. Long-surviving common-pool resource institutions share eight design principles, among them monitoring by users or those accountable to them, graduated sanctions, local conflict resolution and nested layers. Communication and self-chosen sanctions raise cooperation in experiments. Fit to local conditions matters more than the type of regime. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-563](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-563.md)): the Nobel Prize lecture in full, from the Nobel Foundation's PDF. Worth reading as Ostrom's own summary of fifty years of work: polycentricity defined, the eight design principles of long-surviving common-pool resource institutions in their updated form, the experiments on communication and self-chosen sanctions, the field evidence on local monitoring, and the warning against single policy prescriptions. A retrospective lecture, not a report of new results. |
| [LIT-731](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-731.md) | Tiktok's enshittification | Doctorow (2023), Pluralistic, 21 January. Platforms die in three stages: good to users, then abusing users for business customers, then abusing both to take the value for themselves. It follows from the ease of reallocating value in a two-sided market, and lock-in, blocked interoperability and monopoly sustain it. TikTok's "heating" of chosen creators is read as stage two beginning. Remedy: end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-573.md)): in full, from the author's own blog, under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Worth reading as the essay that named enshittification and the earliest statement of it the record holds. Platforms are first good to users, then abuse users for business customers, then abuse both to claw back value; each stage is made possible by the lock-in the last one built, and blocked interoperability raises how much abuse users will bear before leaving. The remedy proposed is end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. Limits: an opinion essay argued from cases, with linked journalism and the author's own experience as evidence; its TikTok claim is a prediction. |
| [LIT-734](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-734.md) | History As Cause: Columbia and Challenger | Columbia Accident Investigation Board (2003), Report Vol. I ch. 8, pp. 195–204. Foam debris and O-ring erosion followed the same trajectory: each anomaly was reinterpreted as acceptable and "in-family", and each flight without disaster justified the next. Budget and schedule pressure, a hierarchy that silenced dissent, and a dependent safety organization sustained the pattern. "History is cause": Challenger's institutional causes had not been fixed. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-578.md)): in full, from the official CAIB report as archived by the UNT Libraries CyberCemetery. Worth reading as the Board's finding that Columbia repeated Challenger's organizational cause: technical anomalies normalized one decision at a time, under budget and schedule pressure, in a hierarchy that kept dissent from rising, with a safety organization dependent on the program it oversaw. Limits: a two-case comparison within one agency, written as an official finding; the chapter is unsigned, and its concept of normalization rests on Vaughan's unread book ([LIT-715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-715.md)). |
| [LIT-736](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-736.md) | Shaping the Institutional Mind | Tollefsen (2025), Philosophies 10(5):112. Advocates and critics of group minds share the "standard view" that ascribing attitudes tracks pre-existing causes. On McGeer's regulative view, ascription shapes its target. Ascribing knowledge to institutions, as in the collective knowledge doctrine, and issuing institutional narratives shape institutions to be more agent-like. The view stays agnostic about whether institutions really have minds. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading for a different answer to why we ascribe beliefs and knowledge to institutions: not because the ascriptions describe pre-existing states, but because, on the regulative view of folk psychology, they shape institutions to be more agent-like. Its main case is the collective knowledge doctrine in corporate criminal law, after which banks built systems to detect reporting violations. Limits: the regulative view is assumed, not argued; the causal story about banks is asserted without evidence; and the paper is agnostic about whether institutions have minds. It does not stand in for her book Groups as Agents ([LIT-483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-483.md)), which stays unread. |
| [LIT-737](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-737.md) | Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action | Ostrom (1990), Cambridge University Press: from case studies of long-enduring and failed common-pool resource institutions, argues that resource users can and do govern commons themselves, without either privatisation or state control, and proposes design principles shared by the institutions that lasted. | [LIT-743](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-743.md) | Risk management in a dynamic society: a modelling problem | Rasmussen (1997), Safety Science 27:183–213. Risk management is a control problem spanning government, regulators, companies, management, staff and work. Behaviour within a work space moves under an effort gradient and a cost gradient toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems, defences degrade unobserved under cost pressure. Accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions. Improvement means making boundaries visible, not fighting errors. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md)): the argument in full, the review of research paradigms skimmed, from the author's manuscript in DTU's repository. Worth reading for the model of drift. Under a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from workers, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems one actor's breach of a defence has no visible effect, so defences erode unobserved. Major accidents come from the interaction of many decision makers adapting to local pressures, not from coincident errors. Built from accident analyses; not a quantitative model. |

His advocacy of voice was "too timid": voice can be felt as a benefit, carries richer information than exit, and suits shared uncertainty; exit can be costly or uninformative. Worth reading as Hirschman's own restatement and extension of Exit, Voice, and Loyalty: voice as a recuperation mechanism that can be a benefit rather than a cost and carries richer information than exit; exit that is costly, or that signals nothing; the floor and ceiling levels of each an organization needs; and managers' interest in steering members toward the least threatening response. | [LIT-752](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-752.md) | The Viable System Model: Its Provenance, Development, Methodology and Pathology | Beer (1984), Journal of the Operational Research Society 35:7–25. A retrospective on the Viable System Model. Any system able to keep its identity independently in a shared environment has five necessary and sufficient subsystems, and every viable system contains and is contained in one. The model is offered as a scientific model reached by homomorphic mapping, not an analogy. Breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem, as when Three and Five collapse without Four. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md)): in full except one page, from the 1989 book reprint posted by the Cwarel Isaf Institute, which Beer co-founded. Worth reading as Beer's own retrospective on the Viable System Model. Five subsystems are claimed necessary and sufficient for any system to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs, since every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns are diagnosed as failures of a subsystem: without System Four, Systems Three and Five collapse into each other and the system can only react. Limits: the paper declines to expound or validate the model, the copy lacks the page with the synopsis of the subsystems and its figures, and the applications are recalled, not documented. |

| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |
